notes: Gaza price lists separate 'رز مصري' (medium/short grain, existing slug rice) from 'رز طويل'/basmati, which costs about 2x as much. Also covers jasmine and parboiled long grain.

aliases_ar: طحين أسمر|دقيق قمح كامل|طحين باب ثاني
notes: Bran oils go rancid faster than white flour; watch for weevils in heat.
Used for basbousa, ma'amoul and harissa sweets; sold loose by the kilo in Gaza.
Fried in oil and cooked with rice, or in soups. Abu Aita 350 g seen in Gaza price lists.
Dried bulgur and flour pearls; homemade versions are sun-dried and keep less long.
Egyptian/North African semolina couscous; less common than maftoul in Gaza.
Boiled whole wheat for bleela (sweet or savoury); needs long cooking, so it uses a lot of gas.
Gaza price lists sell it by the oqiya (وقية, about 250 g) for muhallabiya and puddings.
Sealed boxes/bags. Once opened they go soft quickly in humid air.
Indomie packets and cups appear in Gaza price lists. Cups need only hot water, which saves gas.
Gaza sells 400–500 g boxes (e.g. Pakmaya 450 g) and loose portions. Keeps about a year sealed; once opened it loses strength fast in heat.
Can also be made at home by drying leftover bread.
Twice-baked dry bread, eaten with tea; a good bread stand-in when there is no fresh bread.
Packaged sliced loaf; molds within days in warm, humid shelters.
Baked on hot stones in a taboon oven; often home-baked from aid flour on wood or clay ovens during the war.
Very thin bread baked on a domed saj. It uses little fuel and can be dried to keep longer.
Packaged wraps; low confidence that they are common in Gaza.
Jerusalem-style sesame ring bread from bakeries and street sellers. Gaza 'ka'ak' more often means Eid date cookies, which belong under sweets.
